justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent price level around 624–625, based on typical mean-reversion and momentum dynamics for a mid-to-large cap equity or index-like instrument trading in this range. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price with only a small expected move, since daily returns tend to cluster near zero and there was no strong directional catalyst I weighted heavily. For the 1-week estimate, I allowed for slightly more drift upward, reflecting a mild bullish bias consistent with the broader trend environment. For the 1-month estimate, the drift extends further, though the magnitude remains modest in absolute terms, consistent with historical equity return expectations of roughly 0.5–1% per month in a neutral environment.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized and implied volatility scaling with the square root of time. At the 1-day horizon, a roughly 1.3% half-width on the 90% CI reflects typical daily volatility for this type of instrument. As I extended to 1 week and 1 month, the intervals widened proportionally, though I may have compressed the monthly interval slightly relative to pure volatility scaling to account for some mean-reversion tendencies over longer horizons. The asymmetry in the intervals is intentionally small, reflecting no strong skew signal at the time of the forecast.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include macroeconomic data surprises such as inflation prints, employment reports, or central bank policy shifts, any of which could generate moves of 3–5% or more in a single session. Geopolitical shocks, earnings announcements if this is an individual equity, or sudden liquidity disruptions could also violate the stated bounds. On the upside, a risk-on surge driven by policy easing or stronger-than-expected economic data could push the 1-month outcome well above 695. On the downside, a risk-off episode or sector-specific negative news could easily breach the 575 lower bound.

It is worth emphasizing that these intervals represent my uncertainty at the time of forecasting and are not guarantees. Financial markets can exhibit fat tails and jumps that make even wide 90% confidence intervals insufficient to capture all plausible outcomes. Tail events, by definition, occur more frequently than Gaussian models suggest, and anyone relying on these forecasts for risk management should layer in additional tail-risk considerations beyond what the stated intervals imply.
